title: Why arrangers from inside the band write better for it
summary: Dance objects to albums by a single arranger; Edison says Thad Jones, Frank Wess and Frank Foster knew the band best.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well, I think that, you know, after that *"Flight of the Foo Birds."
atomic album, he did two albums with Benny Carter which I liked.
Yes, yes.
And there was one when Quincy Jones did --
Yeah, that was a good album, too.

That was a good album. But, you know, I often used to argue with Teddy Reig and Willard, I said, "Well, why does he have to have -- when he makes an album, why do you have to have 12 arrangements by one guy?"
Yeah.
If I come to you and say, "Look, I want 12 arrangements by next month," okay, you've got two fresh ideas in your head, which come out pretty good, but the other ten are going to be like hack things.
Uh-huh.
I mean, a lot of the best arrangements, to my mind, came out of that band. I mean, Frank Foster and Frank Wess, --
Yeah, no doubt about it.
-- Thad Jones.
Well, Thad, shoot.
Yeah.
Now he had the best arranger in the world right in the band.
That's it.
Thad. And when you play in a band, you know the ability of everybody in the band.
That's right.
So naturally, you can write for the band better than an outsider, because you're right there at all times.
The outside guys writing for first saxophone and second saxophone.
Oh, yeah, sure.
Don't know who they are.
And Frank Wess was a good writer, Frank Foster is a good writer.
